endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Aggregated metrics: Only metrics representing 10 or more patients may be exported; no proportions that could derive a value less than 10.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Healthcare organizations must ensure that patient data is protected from unauthorized use or release.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Sponsors should provide the recommended information 1502 excluding any patient identifiers, trade secrets, and confidential commercial information.

endorsements.title: Federated data health networks hold potential for accelerating emergency research
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
endorsements.quote: Aggregate analysis is collected by the research center without the need for protected health information to leave individual EDs and generally without the need for data use agreement.

endorsements.title: Promising for patients or deeply disturbing? The ethical and legal aspects of deepfake therapy
endorsements.quote: First, the deepfake and any personal data used for its creation should be stored locally and securely.

evidence.title: A Privacy-Preserving Zero-Code Conversational Statistical Analysis System for Clinical Research Using Agentic AI and Local R Execution
evidence.outcome: Whether row-level patient data stayed local while an external LLM reasoned
evidence.effect: External LLM received zero row-level patient data while all core analytic workflows ran via local R execution in a single MASLD replication; no comparator.
evidence.quote: The external large language model actively clarified analytical prompts while receiving zero row-level patient data.

evidence.title: Advancing Privacy-Preserving Health Care Analytics and Implementation of the Personal Health Train: Federated Deep Learning Study
evidence.outcome: Whether patient-level data stayed inside hospital environments during federated model training
evidence.effect: No data were shared outside the hospital during execution and training across 12 hospitals in 8 nations; a secure aggregation server was used for model averaging.
evidence.quote: During the execution and training of the deep learning algorithm, no data were shared outside the hospital.

evidence.title: K-anonymity decay in multi-turn clinical large language model conversations
evidence.outcome: small-cell threshold crossing in LLM conversations
evidence.quote: Of 5,000 randomly sampled patients, 79.9% (3,994; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 78.8% to 81.0%) reached k < 5 at some point during their disclosure sequence, while 86.2% (4,311; 95% CI: 85.2 to 87.2%) reached k < 11 .
evidence.sample_unit: simulated patients sampled from 133,262 synthetic patients

commentary.bottom_line: Two offline studies found that analytics and federated model training ran without row-level patient data leaving the local environment, but neither tested export review, small-cell suppression, or the handling of embeddings. A separate simulation found that 79.9% of LLM conversations reached k < 5, which shows the disclosure risk exists but does not show that suppression prevents it.

perspectives.view: Two level 4 studies without comparators test only the data-locality part of the recommendation. One replicated a single published study, and the other trained a model across 12 hospitals. Both ran offline or in simulation. No study measured disclosure events, export review, or suppression thresholds, so certainty for the full practice is very low.

A simulation of 5,000 patients found that 79.9% of LLM conversations reached k < 5 and 86.2% reached k < 11. This suggests small-cell exposure may occur routinely in conversational AI outputs. No study tested whether a suppression rule or export review catches these outputs before release.

In one study, an external LLM received zero row-level patient data while core analyses ran through local R execution. In another, federated training across 12 hospitals in 8 nations shared no data outside each hospital. These results suggest that local execution is technically workable. Neither study reported staff burden, workflow fidelity, or how long export review took.

CHAI sets a minimum of 10 patients for exported metrics and bars proportions that could derive smaller values. FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to exclude patient identifiers from submissions. RUAIH guidance requires protection against unauthorized release. The endorsements agree on the principle, but no study tested whether meeting these thresholds prevents re-identification.

The multinational federated study ran across 12 hospitals using a secure aggregation server for model averaging. This suggests that keeping data local can work across sites. The study did not report costs, staffing, or infrastructure requirements, so the resources needed at scale remain unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared export review or small-cell suppression against no review and measured disclosure or re-identification events. No study tested whether embeddings kept inside or exported from the secure environment can be inverted to recover patient data. Studies in live deployments that report staff time and false-positive suppression rates are also missing.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and the multinational study did not describe patient characteristics. Small subgroups produce small cells more often, so suppression rules may disproportionately hide results for these populations. That trade-off between privacy and visibility for these groups has not been measured.
